content: In the passive, the thing that RECEIVES
the action becomes the subject. The
doer steps aside, or vanishes.
Active: They print the magazine weekly.
Passive: The magazine is printed weekly.
Form: be + past participle. The tense
lives in be; the participle stays put.
present: is printed
past: was built
future: will be cleaned
The perfect and continuous work too —
just build be in that tense first:
being built: The bridge is being built.
(passive + continuous)
been done: The work has been done.
(passive + perfect)
To name the doer, add by:
"The magazine is edited by a small team."
Many languages avoid the passive and
keep an active 'one does it' subject;
English lifts the receiver to the front
and lets the doer step aside.
When you arrange for someone ELSE to do
a task, use have/get + thing + done.
"We had the parcel delivered."
= someone delivered it for us; we
arranged it — we did not carry it.
"She got the contract checked."
= a lawyer checked it, at her request.
Form: have/get + the object + past
participle. have is neutral; get is a
little more spoken.
Watch the difference from doing it
yourself:
"I cut my hair." = I did it.
"I had my hair cut." = the barber did.
The same shape can report a mishap:
"They had their car stolen." = it
happened TO them.
Many languages use one plain active verb
and trust the context; English marks
the arranged job with have/get + done.
A relative clause can add EXTRA
information, set off by commas. This is
the non-defining clause.
"The hunter, who had lost his tiger,
searched all night."
The commas mean the clause is extra —
drop it and the sentence still stands:
"The hunter searched all night."
Without commas, the clause instead picks
out WHICH one: "The man who called is
here." (that one, not another).
Never use that in a non-defining clause;
use who or which.
whose shows possession — it replaces
his/her/its/their:
"The hunter, whose tiger had escaped,
raised the alarm."
(the tiger belonged to the hunter)
where points to a place:
"The palace where the maid worked
stood on the hill."
= the palace in which she worked.
Many languages repeat a pronoun ('the
hunter, his tiger...'); English folds
it into one word — whose, where, who —
and joins the two thoughts in one.
